journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: From Ideas to Impact: Mapping Pedagogical Entrepreneurship in the Norwegian Core Curriculum
abstract: In the mid-2000s, Norway aimed to lead in entrepreneurship education, supported by significant political commitment and an action plan. Despite this initial momentum, the post-implementation period saw limited political activity. The new national curriculum, the Knowledge Promotion Reform (LK20) marked a shift, advocating exploration, interdisciplinary work, and deep learning, aligning with pedagogical entrepreneurship’s core. This study analyzes LK20’s expression of pedagogical entrepreneurship using the VECCI-criteria as an analysis framework: Value creation, Experiential learning, Creativity, Collaboration, and Interdisciplinarity. A quantitative content analysis reveals that all the criteria were visible, but Value creation and Experiential learning featured prominently, while Interdisciplinarity was less evident. Qualitative analysis indicates that pedagogical entrepreneurship can help schools meet the core curriculum's goals because its concepts can be applied in various ways. Although there are intentions to fully integrate pedagogical entrepreneurship into the education systems of Norway and Europe, these intentions are not clear in the core curriculum.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Editorial Commentary
abstract: Teacher education is, at its heart, an act of making choices. Decisions about curriculum, assessment, pedagogy, technology, and professional learning all reflect beliefs about what future teachers need to know, what experiences matter, and how they come to develop as professionals. Those decisions are rarely straightforward. They are shaped by local contexts, policy priorities, disciplinary traditions, and the realities of learners themselves. The nine articles in this issue approach these questions from different perspectives, yet each asks how teacher education might better prepare educators to support learning in thoughtful, equitable, and meaningful ways. The majority of the articles published in this issue were first presented at the 2025 International Society for Teacher Education (ISfTE) Seminar hosted by the University of Agder in Kristiansand, Norway. Guided by the theme Teacher Education: Life Skills and Inclusion, the seminar created opportunities for researchers and teacher educators to examine how teacher education can respond to contemporary educational priorities across diverse contexts. This issue also includes manuscripts submitted through JISTE's regular review pr

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: What If Your Mind's Eye Can't See?
abstract: Mental imagery is the ability to create images in the mind. It is a form of visualization where a person perceives an object or scene when the actual object or scene is not present. Most people are surprised to discover that not everyone can create mental images. In 2015, the term aphantasia was coined to refer to the absence of a mind’s eye. Later, the term hyperphantasia was used to describe the opposite end of the mental imagery spectrum, extremely vivid images. The VVIQ is a self-report measure of visual imagery clarity and is often used by researchers to identify aphantasia and hyperphantasia. This study examined the degree to which 4th graders in an elementary school can create mental images. A higher percentage of students in this study were identified with aphantasia and hyperphantasia than in existing research on adults.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Experiences of Fairness in Assessment of Mathematical Modeling Portfolios: Developing Criteria in Collaboration with Preservice Teachers
abstract: This paper addresses fairness of assessment in the context of a developmental project to improve teaching and learning in an introductory mathematical modeling course for preservice teachers (PSTs). Their learning was assessed through a portfolio, and the PSTs and lecturers co-developed the assessment criteria for this portfolio. Through classroom observations and a survey, we analyzed the portfolio assessment and the students’ experiences of the unit in terms of fairness. We conceptualized fairness in terms of coherence and tensions among task demands, opportunities for learning, and transparent assessment. The results indicate that the co-developed assessment criteria were accessible and useful for the PSTs. Together with the portfolio format, the criteria were instrumental in achieving a high level of coherence among task demands, learning opportunities, and transparent assessment.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Investigating Bhutanese Pre-service Teachers' Understanding of and Attitudes Towards Mathematics, Science, and Information Technology (IT) as STEM-Related Subjects
abstract: This study investigates Bhutanese pre-service teachers' attitudes and understanding of STEM-related subjects, with a focus on mathematics, science, and information technology (IT). Although STEM education is gaining importance, most pre-service teachers continue to enroll in non-STEM programs while few STEM graduates pursue teaching, raising concerns about the future quality of STEM education in Bhutan. Using a sequential mixed-methods design, the study collected quantitative (#116) and qualitative (#8) data through questionnaire comprising structured items and an open-ended question, followed by in-depth interviews from the Colleges of Education. Findings reveal generally positive attitudes toward STEM-related subjects but also expose significant gaps in conceptual understanding, suggesting that many pre-service teachers may not be fully prepared to teach STEM-related subjects effectively. The study underscores the need to strengthen content knowledge and pedagogical preparation for STEM-related subjects in teacher education programs to better equip future educators and improve STEM education in Bhutan and comparable developing contexts.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Pre-Service Teachers’ Positioning When Facing Curriculum Change: Incorporating Programming in Science and Mathematics Education
abstract: This study explores pre-service teachers' (PSTs) storylines regarding their engagement with programming as a new component of mathematics and science education in Norwegian schools. To familiarize fourth-year PSTs with programming and exploratory teaching approaches, a 4-week period of experiential learning was conducted. Designed to elicit reflection on the role of the teacher, this 4-week period culminated in the PSTs working in groups to plan and deliver instruction for high school students. We have used narrative inquiry to investigate the positioning of PSTs regarding programming, the use of programming in teaching, and exploratory approaches to teaching programming. The study is based on the weekly reflection logs of nine PSTs. In this paper, we chose one PST (we called Thor, Linn, and Hans) from each group and narrated how their positioning unfolded over the four weeks. Understanding PSTs’ positioning when faced with changing curricula may help teacher educators in supporting prospective teachers.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Digital Stories for Teacher Education: Bhutanese Educators’ Responses to Stories of Bullying and Discrimination
abstract: This study, centering on Bhutanese educators and preservice teachers, explores how digital stories as an arts-based approach can inform culturally responsive teacher education on bullying and discrimination. We examined responses from 56 educators and preservice teachers in Bhutan to three arts-based works. Analysis of these responses generated four themes: developing empathetic understanding, identifying pedagogical applications, recognizing professional development needs, and integrating cultural authenticity. Participants’ responses indicate that digital stories can strengthen emotional competencies, provide practical teaching strategies, and support culturally grounded practice consistent with Bhutan’s Gross National Happiness philosophy. The findings show the potential of arts-based approaches to prepare educators to address diversity, inclusion, and social justice. They also offer a model for international collaboration that honors local values while engaging shared educational challenges.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Building a Scientific Skill Set: A Design-Based Research Approach to Developing a Tool for Science Education and Beyond
abstract: Life skills like problem-solving, communication, collaboration, and creative and critical thinking are closely tied to scientific practices in science education. However, there is ongoing debate about how to define and operationalize scientific practices for implementation in schools and teacher education. In Norway, these practices are a core element of the science curriculum, but their definition remains vague. To address this, we used a design-based research approach to develop a skills-based tool for teaching and learning scientific practices in schools and teacher education. The tool highlights twelve interrelated skills that support students’ engagement in scientific practices and their reflection on scientific processes. We describe the process of designing and developing the teaching tool, our design analysis of why and how the tool evolved, and three design principles to inform the development of a skills-based teaching tool to practice science. These principles highlight three critical features of the tool: it is dynamic and flexible, initiates active learning, and provides support for teachers.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Empowering all Learners: Accessibility of AI Academic Platforms for Students with Disabilities
abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in education presents opportunities to enhance learning, yet its accessibility for students with disabilities (SWD) remains uncertain. This study evaluated 15 AI platforms commonly used in mathematics, language arts, and executive functioning to determine their accessibility and effectiveness for SWD. Using a descriptive non-experimental design, platforms were assessed with a 10-component rubric focused on accessibility, usability, integration with assistive technology, and ethical and equity considerations. Results revealed wide variability in accessibility, with overall scores ranging from 24 to 41 out of 50. While several platforms demonstrated strong instructional potential, most showed limited customizability, unclear privacy practices, and insufficient inclusive design. Findings highlight the need for intentional accessibility features and greater involvement of SWD and educators in AI development to ensure equitable learning outcomes.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Evaluating Behavioral Teaching Strategies for Dance Teachers Working with Neurodiverse Children
abstract: This study evaluated the effectiveness of a recreational dance curriculum titled Dance with a B-E-A-T (Dance with Behaviour Analysis and Therapy) to teach foundational dance skills to neurodiverse children. This curriculum includes evidence-based behavioral teaching strategies (e.g., goal setting, token system) that have been shown to improve learning outcomes for children with and without diverse needs. In our study, three neurodiverse children (7 to 12 years old) participated in eight weekly 1-hour group teaching sessions. A pre-/post-intervention comparison of child learning outcomes was measured using the percentage of steps completed correctly across 10 foundational dance skills. Results showed that the children who participated demonstrated improvements in their overall gross motor performance. Caregivers reported being very satisfied with the program’s effectiveness in preparing neurodiverse children to participate in traditional community dance programs. We highlight the benefits of dance teachers using behavioral teaching strategies to support neurodiverse children in dance programs.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Towards Equity
abstract: This paper critically examines the persistent underrepresentation of Black and racialized pre-service educators in Ontario’s education system, despite the province’s growing student diversity and Canada’s ongoing immigration trends. Drawing on recent research, demographic data, and policy analysis, the review highlights the disparity between Ontario’s diverse student population and the predominantly White teaching workforce. The lack of representative educators not only perpetuates systemic inequities but also affects the academic and social experiences of racialized students. The study identifies institutional barriers, such as a shortage of diverse mentors and inadequate inclusion of equity principles in teacher education programs, that hinder the professional growth of racialized teacher candidates. The paper advocates for a transformative redesign of Ontario’s teacher education programs, emphasizing the comprehensive integration of equity, diversity, inclusion, social justice, anti-racist methods, and culturally sustaining pedagogy to foster a more representative and inclusive teaching workforce.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Facilitators and Constraints of Compassion in Bhutanese Primary Science Teaching
abstract: Limited empirical research has examined how compassion is institutionally supported or constrained within specific practical contexts, and what this means for teacher education. This study investigates primary science teachers’ perceptions of the facilitators and barriers to enacting compassion in Bhutan, a context in which educational policy is shaped by Gross National Happiness values and Buddhist-informed moral education. Findings from analysis of survey and interview data indicate that compassion is significantly enabled by school-based systems as well as by compassionate school leadership. At the same time, teachers identify persistent challenges, including workload pressures, large class sizes, misconceptions equating compassion with leniency, and the relational implications of digital immersion. Interpreted through a teacher education lens, these findings suggest that compassion must be conceptualised as a learnable professional competence requiring explicit preparation, leadership development, and sustained professional learning.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: When Micro Is Not Micro
abstract: Schools in Canada have become a de facto first line of response for young people and their wellbeing needs. In response to teachers’ requests for trauma-informed professional development, we created a virtual microcertificate entitled Trauma-Informed/Sensitive Pedagogies and Practices. We used a mixed-methods approach with a convergent parallel design (Creswell & Plano Clarke, 2018) that draws on quantitative and qualitative data. Data included feedback from teacher participants at any stage of the micro-certificate program, and formal pre- and post-program surveys. Results show this virtual microcertificate can become a complementary pathway to teacher education. As most pre-service teacher education programs across Canada do not offer courses in trauma-informed education, this microcertificate offers an innovative, accessible, and responsive way to invite both pre- and in-service teachers to address this gap in Canada and countries with similar education contexts. Future challenges that we will consider include cost, accessibility, contextual requirements, and crisis response.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Global Perspectives on Teacher Education
abstract: This paper critically examines the evolution and current state of teacher education in Ghana, tracing its historical foundations while addressing contemporary challenges and opportunities. Drawing from our experiences as educators in both Ghanaian and global contexts, we reflect on transforming teacher education to meet the needs of a multicultural society. Emphasizing critical thinking as a tangible and teachable skill, we argue that social justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion—foundational elements that empower teachers to promote just learning environments—should be embedded into curricula. We advocate equipping pre-service teachers to become researchers who continuously improve their practice and enhance student outcomes. Equally critical is the integration of technology to prepare educators for the demands of 21st-century learners while connecting historical insights with forward-looking visions. We call for collaborative efforts to build a transformative and socially responsible teacher education system in Ghana.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Early Childhood Education in Bhutan
abstract: Bhutan, rooted in its unique philosophy of Gross National Happiness, has made significant strides in Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD). This paper provides an overview of the development and current landscape of ECCD in Bhutan in the context of its history of education, especially highlighting the role of teacher education in enhancing the quality of ECCD in Bhutan. ECCD has grown into a national priority, with increasing enrolment, policy development, and institutional support. However, challenges remain, including inadequate facilitator qualifications, gender imbalance of facilitators, and limited inclusivity for children with disabilities. Innovations such as mobile facilitators and ECCD modules in teacher training, alongside a push for a home-grown pedagogy, reflect Bhutan’s commitment to quality and culturally relevant early education. As the nation aligns its ECCD efforts with global commitments like SDG, its vision remains clear: to nurture children through quality education grounded in Bhutanese values and best practices.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Editorial Commentary for the Special Issue
abstract: This special issue brings together fourteen articles examining teacher education across diverse global contexts, including Australia, Bhutan, Canada, Cyprus, Ghana, Japan, Mexico, Nigeria, Norway, Serbia, and the United States. The collection explores how teacher education systems are shaped by local histories, policies, and priorities, while addressing shared challenges such as equity, professional preparation, and educational change. Together, the articles offer a comparative and contextually grounded understanding of the complexities, innovations, and tensions shaping teacher education worldwide.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Teacher Education in Nova Scotia
abstract: Teacher education in Nova Scotia has developed through a distinctive historical trajectory, beginning with the Provincial Normal School and evolving into today’s university-based programs. This paper examines how historical shifts, political decisions, and policy reforms continue to shape teacher preparation in the province. Current challenges include teacher shortages, the tension between accelerated pathways and rigorous preparation, and the under-representation of Indigenous and African Nova Scotian educators. We highlight initiatives that address these challenges, including Acadia University’s Africentric Bachelor of Education program and Indigenous teacher pathways. Course-level innovations at St. Francis Xavier University further emphasize critical reflection, reconciliation, and social justice. By situating these developments within broader Canadian reforms and equity movements, the paper shows how Nova Scotia’s experience reflects both enduring legacies and emerging innovations in preparing teachers for diverse and inclusive classrooms.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: A Programmatic Approach to Help Teacher Candidates View Themselves as Global Citizens
abstract: In the US, the process of educating elementary and secondary children is not fully federally funded. The US Department of Education (DOE) oversees a portion of educational funding through the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA), the primary federal law governing public education of school-aged children. ESEA’s focus has historically been around educational equity and requires schools’ accountability for student success through assessments in reading, math, and science. ESEA only provides a small portion for children’s education and the majority of educational funding and decision-making is given to the states. Each state has its own educational standards, and curriculum is most often handled at the local/regional level. In the wake of the new presidential administration’s call to dismantle the DOE, the small portion of federal education funding has been called into question, with a push to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusive (DEI) focused programs. Some of the more conservative states have required eliminating DEI language in their standards and prohibited curriculum and programming that address these ideals. This paper addresses the educational landscape in one of

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Indigenous Teacher Education in Sonora, Mexico
abstract: This research investigates teacher education practices serving the Comcáac (Seri) community in Sonora, Mexico, in the coastal region near Kino Bay. As Mexico's smallest Indigenous group, the Comcáac people inhabit two coastal towns: Punta Chueca (Socaaix) and Desemboque (Haxöl Iihom). This research examines how teacher preparation addresses this community's cultural needs. Literature revealed significant obstacles: limited resources, few native-language speakers in teaching programs, and insufficient culturally responsive pedagogies. However, promising developments emerged through community-led teacher training and innovative partnerships between formal institutions and traditional knowledge systems. While Mexico's intercultural education policies appear robust, implementation gaps persist for smaller Indigenous populations. Future teacher preparation must integrate climate education, enhanced digital literacy, and sustainable community-educator partnerships. These approaches should honor traditional ecological knowledge while preparing students for contemporary challenges beyond their ancestral territories. This research contributes to understanding how teacher education can bette

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Global Perspectives on Teacher Education: Innovations and Challenges in International Contexts
abstract: A new national curriculum (LK20) was implemented in Norway in 2020, which integrates three cross-curricular themes: Public Health and Life Skills, Democracy and Citizenship, and Sustainable Development. The introduction of these three themes must be understood in the Norwegian national teacher education landscape due to their ability to shape societal development. Research has uncovered challenges and opportunities in teacher education such as teachers’ experiences of responsibility for deliverables that go beyond their competence. The Norwegian teacher program was elevated to a five-year master’s degree in 2017, underpinning the strength of a high professional standard and research-based teaching, and the close partnership with schools which enables innovative and interdisciplinary perspectives. To meet the increasing demands placed on teachers, the teacher education vision for the future needs to be adaptive and embrace the importance of a cross-curricular themes, to facilitate relevant student learning which will support students to face tomorrow’s challenges.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Australia and the urgent need to establish Culturally Nourishing Schooling practices
abstract: In Australia, as in other settler colonial contexts, First Nations students have historically been poorly served by the education system. Since the 1970s, education policies have aimed to address this dire situation, but efforts to support these policies have yielded limited positive results. Teachers have long voiced concerns, including a lack of confidence, limited access to resources, disinterest, or reluctance to assume this responsibility. Negative perceptions of First Nations learners and communities continue to influence both the education sector and the wider public. In recent years, considerable hope has been placed on approaches that are culturally responsive as a way forward. Our work in this area has been connected with the Culturally Nourishing Schooling (CNS) project, a whole-school reform initiative designed to base educational practices within local contexts, and thus relies on reimagining communication, collaboration, and relationships that are no longer hindered by settler illiteracy. Therefore, our vision for teacher education actively promotes settler literacy across the nation and beyond.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Navigating the Future
abstract: Teacher education in Nigeria stands at the crossroads of global transformation and local realities. While education systems worldwide are under pressure to adapt to ideas like globalisation and digitalisation, Nigerian teacher preparation struggles with deep-rooted structural issues. This research was designed to critically examine how Nigerian teacher education can navigate these shifts. Employing a qualitative research design, thematic content analysis was used on various documents to identify recurring issues and promising practices, allowing for both national insights and global discourse. Findings reveal that Nigerian teacher education has many lingering constraints. However, the research also identified several areas of innovation. Although practices are uneven and often donor-driven, they point to a sector that is slowly responding to global trends. Conclusions suggest that sustained investment, coherent policies, and contextualised adoption of global best practices are essential to revitalising Nigerian teacher education.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: An Overview of Teacher Education in Serbia
abstract: With a history dating back to the late 18th century, teacher preparation programs in Serbia have transitioned from more traditional pedagogical models to modern frameworks aligned with the European Bologna Process. This paper highlights the challenges teacher preparation in Serbia faces, including significant teacher shortages, low salaries, and a lack of centralized consistency in professional practice across universities. At the same time, we discuss many innovative initiatives, such as digital pedagogy and AI integration. Drawing comparisons with international models, the paper argues for a multifaceted reform of teacher preparation in Serbia. Recommendations include elevating teachers' social status by increasing financial investment, modernizing schools, and standardizing hands-on clinical practice. Finally, the paper posits that the sustainability of national well-being in Serbia depends on a fundamental reinvestment in the recruitment and training of its educators.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Traditions and Challenges in Japan’s Teacher Education
abstract: The main purpose of this paper is to suggest the traditional and current status in Japan’s teacher education from an international perspective in order to contribute to the global advancement of this field. This paper specifically consists of following sequence: 1. Historical Background of Teacher Education in Japan: Before the War, after the War, and into the Present, 2. Open System and Teacher Certification System as Fundamental Frame of the Current Teacher Education, 3. Policy Trends since the 2000s: Transformation of School Management and Alternative Pathways to Teaching Profession, 4.Current Challenges by Failure of Centralized Reforms: Facing Threat of Teaching Profession, 5. Suggestions of Latent Potential that Run Counter to the Mainstream. Insight into its historical development is essential in order to understand teacher education substantially. The inevitable gap between the ideals inherent in social institutions and their reality must be also critically examined. Regarding Japan’s teacher education, the focus extends beyond the stated principles of the system to the culture that shapes reality and the resulting facts. This paper aims to reposition Japanese teacher educa

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Reframing Pedagogical Foundations
abstract: This paper critically examines the historical trajectory, current challenges, and prospects of teacher education in Cyprus, offering a reframed understanding of its pedagogical foundations. Drawing on policy analysis, scholarly literature, and sociocultural perspectives, the study traces the evolution of teacher preparation programs from colonial legacies to contemporary reforms aligned with European standards. It interrogates persistent issues such as centralized curricula, limited autonomy in teacher practice, and the tensions between traditional pedagogies and progressive educational ideals. By situating Cyprus within broader global discourses on education reform, the paper highlights how localized challenges—such as multicultural settings, migration and refugees, and shifting social expectations—complicate efforts to modernize teacher education. The paper concludes with a call for a more reflective, contextually responsive, and critically engaged approach to shaping the next generation of educators in Cyprus.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Bhutanese Elementary Teachers’ Assessment Conceptions
abstract: The purpose of this study was to investigate Bhutanese elementary teachers' conceptions about assessments to determine teachers’ inclination towards improving conceptions (formative) or accountability conceptions (summative). Assessment conceptions were measured using the abridged version of CoA-III Abridged (CoA-III A) inventory proposed by Brown (2006) which includes four pre-determined assessment conceptions: assessment for improvement, assessment for student accountability, assessment for school accountability, and assessment as an irrelevance. The data was collected from 111 elementary teachers using an online survey questionnaire. Findings indicate that teachers conceive that the purpose of assessments is for improvement. They also conceived of assessments as irrelevant. There was a strong positive correlation between the conception of assessments for improvement and student accountability and a positive association between improvement and irrelevance conceptions. It was concluded that teachers have positive conceptions about assessment, but they often experience an assessment practice dilemma between the improvement and accountability purposes of assessment.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Through the Eyes of a Visitor: A Different Perspective on Teaching
abstract: Educators and teacher educators can develop blind spots to professional ideas and issues. Objectivity may come through the eyes of someone outside the profession. This study looked at a higher education advisor studying education, but who had no intention to apply for licensure nor to teach. She participated in a materials development project to create culturally-appropriate electronic learning materials for Thai children. During the project, the participant reflected on not only developing materials for teaching but also teaching itself. In this study, we examined and triangulated the reflective journals, interviews, journal reflection and final philosophy statement of the participant. The data showed that she expressed ideas related to the profession of teaching that the education majors in the project did not express. The findings provide insights that can inform both English as a Second Language (ESL) teaching specifically, and teacher education more broadly.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Editorial Commentary: Teacher Learning in Transition: Reflections on Practice, Assessment, and Innovation
abstract: This issue of the Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education (JISTE) brings together six articles from Norway, the United States and Bhutan that explore the shifting landscape of teacher learning, professional development, and pedagogical transformation. The issue spotlights how teacher educators and in-service teachers are grappling with emerging demands - from integrating educational technologies and facilitating complex mathematics instruction, to re-evaluating assessment practices and addressing entrenched norms in teacher education. The authors draw on diverse research methods, including reflective self-study, case study, survey research, and discourse analysis, to examine the tensions, insights, and innovations emerging within teacher education programs and classrooms across global contexts. As teacher roles evolve in response to sociocultural, technological, and policy shifts, the articles in this issue provide critical perspectives on how educators are learning to navigate these transitions. Together, they invite readers to consider the value of reflective practice, digital engagement, and pedagogical flexibility in building responsive and inclusive educatio

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Impact of Nearpod on Students’ Motivation and Learning about Minerals: A Case Study
abstract: This study examines the impact of Nearpod on students’ motivation and learning outcomes about minerals. The study adopted a quantitative method; a pre-experimental design type of one-group pretest-posttest design, whereby one group of grade 10 students (n=24) was taken as a sample. An observation tool was used to study students’ motivational behavior, and a two-tier multiple-choice diagnostic instrument was employed to assess student learning outcomes. The findings indicate that using interactive digital tools positively influenced students’ motivation to learn and increased their participation in the learning process. Furthermore, the study found that using digital technology enhances students’ understanding of the subject matter as evidenced by a significant improvement in the mean marks of the students in the post-test. The findings of this research suggest that the integration of interactive digital tools into the classroom can enhance student’s learning experiences and academic performance.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Thrown into the Deep End: K-12 Teachers’ Educational Technology Usage in Utah During the Pandemic
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic's shift to emergency remote teaching (ERT) revealed significant gaps in K-12 teachers' preparedness to use educational technology (ET) outside traditional settings. This study explores ET usage among Utah's K-12 teachers in 2021, focusing on tool prevalence, differences between elementary and secondary educators, and variations by educational attainment. A survey of 5,934 teachers resulted in 902 responses. Findings indicate that while traditional tools like printers and projectors were widely used, newer technologies such as Canvas and Zoom became essential. Some differences also emerged between groups. The study highlights the need for comprehensive ET training to prepare teachers for diverse instructional environments and informs recommendations for teacher preparation and professional development programs.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Preservice Mathematics Teachers’ Discourse on Proof-Based Teaching in an Online Discussion Forum
abstract: Proof and proving play a fundamental role in mathematics education and have the potential to serve as a vehicle for developing a deeper conceptual understanding. However, engaging students in proving activities presents challenges, and mathematics teacher educators thus are responsible for supporting preservice teachers, providing opportunities to learn what is needed. This study employs an exploratory case study design, investigating preservice teachers' discourse on proof-based teaching within a Norwegian university mathematics course preparing them to teach algebra and number theory (grades 5–10). Data were collected from weekly instructor-initiated online discussions, where preservice teachers reflected on their experiences with proof-based teaching. Through content analysis of data, characteristics of the preservice teachers' discourse on proof-based teaching were explored, revealing dynamic interactions centred around key themes related to proof-based teaching. Interactive patterns emerging in the online discussion forum indicate how these preservice teachers are gradually developing into reflective practitioners.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Challenges and Perceptions of Mathematical Modelling Among Norwegian Pre-Service Teachers
abstract: Mathematical modelling can be described as “[…] the process of translating between the real world and mathematics in both directions” (Blum & Ferri, 2009, p. 45). Both students and teachers often find mathematical modelling challenging. Thus, it is important that future teachers are aware of the challenges their students might encounter when working on this topic. Based on observations and interviews, this study examines obstacles that Norwegian pre-service teachers face in mathematical modelling, and how they perceive their own solution process after learning about mathematical modelling. The study draws on a seven-step modelling cycle described by Blum (2015), and reveals that the pre-service teachers, due to the lack of assumptions, struggle to give meaningful interpretations of their mathematical results. Their perceptions about having to provide their answer as a general expression, are found to be related to their expectations stemming from classroom activities different from student-centered modelling sessions.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Using Behavior Analysis and Therapy to Teach Dance to Neurodiverse Children in Day Treatment Education Program
abstract: Neurodiverse children in day treatment programs often experience behavioral challenges that limit their opportunities to engage in recreational physical activities. These activities are important for physical health and aid in developing motor and socio-emotional skills. The present study used an explanatory sequential mixed methods design to evaluate the effectiveness of Dance With A B-E-A-T! (Behavior-Analysis-and-Therapy), a community-based program combining dance with applied behavior analysis (e.g., modeling, reinforcement), to teach three dance sequences to five neurodiverse participants (7-9 years) in a day treatment program. journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Identity Shifts of Content Area Teachers in the Early Stages of English as Second Language Professional Development Program
abstract: Teachers’ professional identities are continuously being shaped by new knowledge gained through continued coursework and professional development (PD). Traditionally, PD programs and coursework tend to focus on assets such as knowledge or competencies but forego helping students answer questions about their professional identity. This study examines the professional identity development of content-area teachers earning an English as a Second Language endorsement in an online PD program. Using thematic analysis to analyze reflective writings, the researchers examine the identity development of these teachers. Even with the short duration of the PD, changes in professional identity occurred. Shifts included participants’ views on appropriate methods and instructional strategies in the ELL classrooms, their contextual understanding to support ELLs based on their teaching experience and pedagogical approaches, and their overall perception about the social constructs ELLs are experiencing. The change allowed the participants to increase their effectiveness in working with ELLs.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Sustaining Students’ Interest and Engagement in Learning School Science During Interactive Lectures
abstract: How do teachers elicit and sustain students’ interest and engagement in science lessons? This paper answers this question in the context of Bhutan, where students’ performance in science is low compared to other subjects, and where falling levels of interest in science are a concern. Like other countries in the Global South, a large proportion of science lessons are delivered through interactive lectures. Data were generated from observation of 78 grade 6, 8 and 10 science lessons at a Bhutanese middle secondary school, complemented by interviews with 4 students in each grade and their teachers. Teachers’ questioning techniques were key to interactive lectures that students found interesting and engaging. Using Krapp’s Person-Object theory of Interest (POI), questioning practices were analyzed in terms of cognitive challenges, autonomy, cognitive dissonance, and novelty. This paper offers new insights into science pedagogies for contexts where interactive lectures remain common pedagogical practice.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: How Can My Role Support You in Your Role? Collaborative Practices from the Perspective of an Elementary Teacher and a School Social Worker
abstract: Recent data from the National Center for Education Statistics indicates that the COVID-19 pandemic has significantly affected students’ academic performance and overall well-being, creating a rise in mental health needs. In response to this, there has been an increase in hiring school-based social workers. However, there is a lack of clarity on roles and responsibilities and the types of specific collaborative activities teachers and school social workers engage in. This paper presents two case studies featuring a teacher’s perspective on collaborating with a social worker and a social worker’s perspective with a teacher in their respective elementary schools. The case studies showcase successful collaborative activities and address challenges faced by both professionals.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: About This Issue
abstract: This issue of the Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education (JISTE), titled Fostering Inclusive and Reflective Pedagogies: Advancing Education Through Equity, Collaboration, and Student Engagement, explores innovative and diverse approaches to teacher education by reflecting on the intersection of identity, collaboration, student motivation, and inclusive pedagogies across global contexts. Featuring case studies, research, and reflective essays from Bhutan, Ghana, Canada, and the United States, the articles address key topics such as equitable disciplinary practices, the inclusion of neurodiverse learners, and interdisciplinary collaboration between educators and support staff. Emphasizing the importance of culturally responsive teaching, professional development, and reflective practice, this issue highlights how these approaches foster student engagement and enhance educational outcomes. By examining how varied national contexts respond to the challenges and opportunities in contemporary education, this issue provides valuable insights for educators, researchers, and policymakers.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Transforming Student Discipline: A Teacher’s Reflective Essay on Moving From Punishment to Compassion in Education
abstract: In this reflective essay, I examine the impact of corporal punishment in Ghanaian schools by drawing on my experiences as both a victim and a former perpetrator of these practices. Through reflecting on the punitive discipline I endured and later enforced, I highlight the detrimental effects on students’ well-being, self-worth, and engagement in learning. Guided by Parker J. Palmer’s (1997, 2015) concept that “we teach who we are,” I point out the need for educators to embody compassion, empathy, and self-awareness. I also advocate for eliminating punitive discipline in favor of nurturing, supportive, and non-violent relationships that consider the broader socioeconomic and personal contexts influencing student behavior. By creating, sustaining, and promoting a caring, inclusive, and empowering school environment, I argue that teachers can address the cycle of fear and humiliation that stifles student engagement and instead create a space where students feel valued and motivated to develop their full potential.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: Secondary Students’ Motivation Levels and Factors influencing Motivations through the Lens of Self-determination Theory
abstract: This study examines the levels of motivation among secondary school students in learning geography, as well as the factors influencing their motivation. Utilizing a convergent mixed-methods design, data was collected through survey questionnaires and focus group discussions. The quantitative findings indicated a high level of motivation among students, supported by qualitative findings revealing intrinsic and extrinsic motivations such as interest in the subject. Factors influencing motivation included teaching strategies, teacher attributes, and teacher-student relationships. Moreover, interactive teaching methods, friendly and approachable teachers, and positive teacher-student relationships emerged as significant influencers of student motivation. This study contributes to the understanding of motivational factors in the context of geography learning, providing insights for educators and policymakers to optimize teaching practices and curriculum design. The present study concludes with practical implications, limitations of the study and recommendations.

journal_name: Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education
title: About This Issue
abstract: Welcome to Volume 28, Number 1 of the Journal of the International Society for Teacher Education (JISTE). This issue features articles that were presented at the 2023 Annual ISfTE Seminar in Bhutan, hosted by Kezang Sherab and Ugyen Choden at the Royal University of Bhutan under the theme "Education in the Post Covid-19 Pandemic." We are delighted to include these and other contributions from our International Society for Teacher Education (ISfTE) members in this edition. Together, the articles in this issue cover various aspects of education and teaching, including innovative lesson planning methods, frameworks for reviewing primary education, holistic skill development programs, revised assessment models for pre-service teachers, and the importance of teacher dispositions in inclusive education. These studies emphasize enhancing educational practices, fostering growth in both teachers and students, and applying context-specific solutions to improve learning outcomes.
